evergreen_facts.text: Paris takes its name from the Parisii, a Celtic people who lived along the Seine before the Romans arrived.
The storming of the Bastille in Paris on 14 July 1789 is commemorated each year as France's national day.
The Eiffel Tower in Paris was built as the centerpiece of the 1889 World's Fair.
Work on Notre-Dame de Paris, the Gothic cathedral on the Île de la Cité, began in 1163.
The Louvre in Paris was a royal palace before it opened as a museum in 1793; it is home to the Mona Lisa.
The Arc de Triomphe in Paris was commissioned by Napoleon in 1806 to honor the French army.
The Seine divides Paris into the Right Bank to the north and the Left Bank to the south.
Paris is divided into 20 arrondissements that spiral outward clockwise from the center of the city.
Many Paris Métro entrances keep their Art Nouveau ironwork designed by Hector Guimard around 1900.
The Académie Française, founded in Paris in 1635, is the official guardian of the French language.
The baguette is a daily staple in Paris, and French baguette baking is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
The croque monsieur, a toasted ham and cheese sandwich, first appeared on Paris café menus in 1910.
Louis Pasteur founded the Pasteur Institute in Paris in 1887 to study and fight infectious disease.
Marie Curie carried out her Nobel Prize-winning research on radioactivity in Paris.
The Tour de France, first raced in 1903, traditionally ends in Paris on the Champs-Élysées.
The French Open tennis championship is played on red clay courts at Stade Roland Garros in Paris.
